description: A small to medium deciduous tree 8-18 m tall with feathery-looking leaflets arranged along slender twigs, tiny greenish flowers and firm, pale green, six-lobed fleshy fruits that taste sour, bitter and astringent.
cultural_significance: Amalaki is one of the three fruits of Triphala and is revered as 'Dhatri' (the nurse or mother). Amla Navami is a festival where the tree is worshipped. Not a Vedic-era plant by name with certainty; prominent in the Samhitas and Nighantus.
habitat: Dry deciduous forests and plains of the Indian subcontinent; widely cultivated in orchards, especially in Uttar Pradesh and Gujarat.

uses.title: Rasayana (rejuvenative) tonic
uses.detail: Amalaki is described as the foremost Rasayana fruit, used in Chyawanprash and other tonics for vitality and ageing.

uses.title: Digestion and acidity
uses.detail: The fruit is traditionally used to support digestion, to ease hyperacidity and as a mild laxative in Triphala.

uses.title: Hair and eye care
uses.detail: Amla oil and powder are traditionally used for scalp health and hair greying; the fruit is described as Chakshushya (good for eyes).

uses.title: Vitamin C source
uses.detail: Fresh fruit is a rich dietary source of vitamin C and polyphenols; used as food, pickle and preserve.

uses.title: Blood sugar and cholesterol research
uses.detail: Early studies suggest amla extracts may help lipid and glucose levels; evidence is preliminary.

classical_refs: Charaka Samhita - listed among Vayahsthapana (age-sustaining) herbs

preparations.name: Fresh fruit or juice
preparations.method: Eat the raw fruit with a pinch of salt or press the juice and dilute with water.
preparations.note: Sour and cooling; may be uncomfortable on an empty stomach for some.

preparations.name: Amalaki churna (powder)
preparations.method: Dry fruit pulp, powder and take with water or honey as traditionally advised.
preparations.note: Often combined with other herbs in Triphala.

preparations.name: Chyawanprash
preparations.method: A classical herbal jam made by cooking amla pulp with ghee, sugar and many other herbs.
preparations.note: Contains sugar; mind it in diabetes.

preparations.name: Amla oil
preparations.method: Dry amla simmered in coconut or sesame oil and applied to the scalp.

precautions: May lower blood sugar and slow blood clotting, so people on diabetes or anticoagulant medicines, or before surgery, should consult a doctor. Its sour, cooling nature may aggravate cold or acidity in some; avoid large amounts in pregnancy without advice. Rarely causes loose stools in excess.

cultivation.climate: Tropical to subtropical; tolerates heat and mild frost
cultivation.soil: Well-drained loam; tolerates saline and poor soils, pH 6-8
cultivation.propagation: Grafting or budding of selected varieties; seeds for rootstock
cultivation.harvest: Fruits ripen from October to February

fun_fact: Amla is among the richest natural sources of vitamin C and its vitamin content is reported to survive drying better than most fruits, partly due to its tannins.

regions.name: Gangetic Plains
regions.note: Major orchard belt in Uttar Pradesh

regions.name: Sri Lanka
regions.note: Native in dry zone and home gardens
